1.pericope_label: Run ye to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, and see now, and know
debates: Who is told to make the search
Whether the picture suits the reign it is dated to
How men who swore by the divine name could still be perjured
outliers: Ellicott allows that the prophecy may have been reworked later, or else that the prophet saw the reformation of his day was hollow at the time
Wesley notes that God offers to pardon for one righteous man where he once came no lower than ten
themes: A city searched street by street for one man
Truth fallen in the street and seeking corners
The most solemn oath used for perjury
A pardon offered on a condition none can meet

3.pericope_label: O Lord, are not thine eyes upon the truth? thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved
debates: What the truth God looks for consists in
Why the prophet turns from the people to address God
Whether the plea of ignorance for the poor is meant sincerely
outliers: Calvin warns that the chapter divisions themselves have misled interpreters, and would keep the numbers only as an aid to memory
Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin both read the plea for the poor as a device that sets up the discovery of worse guilt higher up
themes: A God who sees through every mask
A prophet who breaks off and speaks to rocks
People too busy earning bread to be taught
No soundness from the head to the sole

5.pericope_label: I will get me unto the great men, and will speak unto them; for they have known the way of the Lord
debates: Whether the three beasts are literal or stand for invaders
Whether the sixth verse looks forward or back
Whether the wolf belongs to the evening or the desert
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch denies both the figurative and the future reading, and takes the verbs of chastisements already partly suffered
Clarke supports the charge against the great with an ancient saying that laws are cobwebs which the great break through
themes: Irony in repeating a compliment that was not earned
Restraint cast off by the men who knew better
Three beasts for three kinds of cruelty
A wolf maddened by a day of fruitless hunting

7.pericope_label: How shall I pardon thee for this? thy children have forsaken me, and sworn by them that are no gods
debates: What force the opening question carries
Whether the clause means fed to the full or bound by oath
Whether the adultery charged is literal or idolatrous
outliers: Ellicott prefers the Hebrew text over the marginal reading and gets bound them by oath instead of fed them to the full
Calvin distinguishes divine from human pardon, since God pardons only by leading a man to repent
themes: A judge inviting the accused to give the verdict
A covenant treated as a marriage bond
A single house standing for a whole apostasy
A word too difficult for its translators

10.pericope_label: Go ye up upon her walls, and destroy; but make not a full end
debates: Whether the words mean walls and battlements or palm trees and branches
Why the destruction is limited
What the charge of treachery amounts to
outliers: Ellicott reads the whole verse as arboreal imagery and notes that palm and vine both served later as national symbols
Clarke reports an old reading that leaves the foundations because they are the Lord own
themes: An enemy mustered like a herald at command
High walls that only make a longer climb
A stem cut down and a root spared
Two rival houses agreeing in one thing

12.pericope_label: They have belied the Lord, and said, It is not he; neither shall evil come upon us
debates: Whether they lied to God or denied him outright
What the clause it is not he denies
Whose voice speaks the last clause of the thirteenth verse
outliers: Calvin settles the charge by the preposition, and collects the other places where the verb takes the same construction
Ellicott renders the closing clause as a wish, so that the mockers call the prophets threatenings down on the prophets themselves
themes: Providence denied without a word said against God
A conclusion valid on its own false premises
The majesty of God tied to the preaching of it
Threats dismissed as so much wind

14.pericope_label: Because ye speak this word, behold, I will make my words in thy mouth fire, and this people wood, and it shall devour them
debates: Who the nation from far is, and which empire is meant
Whether the house of Israel here means the twelve tribes or Judah alone
What sense of fire is intended when the word is called fire
outliers: Calvin distinguishes this fire from the cleansing fire of the word elsewhere, and makes it purely consuming
Ellicott gives the adjective rendered mighty the strict force of lasting or enduring
themes: Words dismissed as air, returned as fire
A tongue alone more than sufficient to destroy a people
Antiquity of empire breeding ferocity
A speech that cannot be understood, and so cannot be entreated

16.pericope_label: Their quiver is as an open sepulchre, they are all mighty men
debates: Whether the open sepulchre means unerring aim or bottomless capacity
Whether the sons and daughters are eaten or only deprived of food
Whether not making a full end is mercy held back or vengeance held in reserve
outliers: Calvin says nearly all interpreters read the closing verse as hope, and he knows no one who takes his own severer view
Ellicott removes the relative pronoun and makes the children objects of the devouring
Calvin rejects the reading of marksmanship and makes the figure one of sheer capacity
themes: A grave that is never satisfied
Feigned flight and the arrow loosed in turning
The harvest given as fodder to the horses
Rest supposed, and the scourge still in reserve

19.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, when ye shall say, Wherefore doeth the LORD our God all these things unto us?
debates: Whether the question is the beginning of repentance or the murmur of hypocrites
Whether the command to declare is a herald proclaiming war or a prophet urging fear
To whom the plural imperatives are addressed
outliers: Ellicott ends a section here and reads the question as a backward glance bringing repentance
Gill takes the plural verbs as an order to declare war rather than a word to the prophet
Wesley narrows Judah and Jacob to the two tribes only
themes: A punishment that can be read backwards into the sin
Innocence pleaded with an iron front
War proclaimed by heralds that the cause might appear just
Strange gods at home answered by strangers abroad

21.pericope_label: Hear now this, O foolish people, and without understanding; which have eyes, and see not; which have ears, and hear not
debates: Whether the eyes and ears are a concession or an irony
Why the sand rather than the rock is the sea bound
Whether the verb means they defy or they turn away
outliers: Calvin argues the restraint of the sea from the sphericity of the element and its lightness relative to the earth
Ellicott hears in the passage the wonder of an inland dweller unused to the sight of surf
Calvin prefers the future tense throughout, making the blindness a refusal rather than a defect
themes: Eyes that have their use and will not use it
A barrier of loose grains that no wave displaces
Wildest force held under an overruling law
A will that alone in creation can refuse

24.pericope_label: Neither say they in their heart, Let us now fear the LORD our God, that giveth rain, both the former and the latter, in his season
debates: Whether the land has two distinct rainy seasons or one long one
Whether the word means appointed weeks or a sufficiency
Why the bounty of God is not evident enough to compel gratitude
outliers: Ellicott names a shift in the argument, from law amid lawless elements to regularity of succession
Clarke reports a rendering that turns the weeks into a sufficiency, resting on a change of sibilant, and rejects it
Calvin answers the objection that seasons are disordered by saying our sins are what disorder them
themes: A thought that never once came into the mind
Bread eaten without a thought of who gave it
Rain divided by its office, one for sowing and one for ripening
Heavens turned to brass and earth to iron

26.pericope_label: For among my people are found wicked men: they lay wait, as he that setteth snares; they set a trap, they catch men
debates: Whether the wicked men are a party within the people or the people themselves
Whether the cage is a keeping-basket or a decoy trap
Whose prospering is meant in the closing clause
outliers: Calvin says the interpreters who confine the charge to some among the people have mistaken it
Ellicott reads the singular and plural verbs as isolated guilt and confederate evil
Clarke turns the last clause into a question, and shall they prosper
themes: A fowler lying down out of sight beside his net
Tame birds set out to bring the wild ones down
Houses full not of fraud but of what fraud fetched
Splendour that dazzles the eyes of the simple

29.pericope_label: Shall I not visit for these things? saith the LORD: shall not my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?
debates: Whether the horrible thing looks back over the chapter or forward to the last verse
Whether the priests ruled by the prophets or applauded them
What the end thereof is the end of
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch treats the last two verses as an addition made after the chapter had reached its conclusion
Ellicott reports a rendering in which the priests applaud with their hands, reversing who leads whom
Calvin holds that the world is never deceived except with its own consent
themes: A question asked twice because it was not heard once
A wrong no words can carry and no mind take in
Prophets and priests each keeping the other in place
Blind guides followed willingly
